system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 4 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2145-08-04 10:30:00 to 2145-08-07 11:43:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of recurrent lower extremity cellulitis, chronic ulcers, and multiple comorbidities was admitted for worsening cellulitis around a left ankle ulcer, with copious drainage and spreading erythema. She had recently failed to complete a prior course of IV vancomycin due to PICC line dislodgement. IV vancomycin was restarted, and a new PICC line was placed on hospital day 3 with confirmed appropriate positioning on chest imaging. The infection showed clinical improvement during the admission, with reduced redness, swelling, and drainage. The right ankle was monitored for possible early cellulitis but remained stable. She was discharged home with home health services to complete antibiotic therapy and wound care, with follow-up planned with dermatology and her gerontologist.
problems: Cellulitis and abscess of leg, except foot
Methicillin susceptible Staphylococcus aureus in conditions classified elsewhere and of unspecified site
Other specified bacterial infections in conditions classified elsewhere and of unspecified site, other specified bacteria
Osteoarthrosis, unspecified whether generalized or localized, site unspecified
Spinal stenosis, lumbar region, without neurogenic claudication
Disorder of bone and cartilage, unspecified
Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism

medications cannot be called into your pharmacy and must be 
picked up in the clinic or mailed to your ___.  Please allow 
an extra 2 days if you would like your medication mailed to your 
home.
 
5. You may not drive a car until cleared to do so by your 
surgeon.

follow-up appointment in three (3) weeks.

especially after activity or physical therapy. Do not place ice

anti-inflammatory medications (NSAIDs such as Celebrex, 
ibuprofen, Advil, Aleve, Motrin, naproxen etc).
 
8. ANTICOAGULATION: Please continue your Lovenox for four (4) 
weeks to help prevent deep vein thrombosis (blood clots).  If 
you were taking aspirin prior to your surgery, it is OK to 
continue at your previous dose while taking this medication.

dry. REMOVE on ___. It is okay to shower five days after 
surgery but no tub baths, swimming, or submerging your incision 
until after your four (4) week checkup. You may place a dry 
sterile dressing on the wound after the Silverlon dressing is 
removed, otherwise leave it open to air. Check wound regularly 
for signs of infection such as redness or thick yellow drainage. 
Staples will be removed by at your follow-up visit in 3 weeks.
 
10. ___ (once at home): Home ___, dressing changes as 
instructed, and wound checks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Patel, one of the orthopedic surgeons. You’re here today for a revision of your right knee replacement, specifically the tibial component, because it’s become loose and is causing you pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the pain’s been getting worse over the past few years. I can barely walk without it hurting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. The X-rays confirmed loosening and a bit of deformity in your leg. We’ll replace that part of the implant today. The surgery is planned and you’ll be taken to the OR shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be under general anesthesia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll be fully asleep. You’ll also get antibiotics through your IV before the surgery to prevent infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve had infections before, so I’m a little worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know about your history—past cellulitis and wound infections. That’s why we’re being extra careful with antibiotics and monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. And my prednisone—I take it for polymyalgia—should I keep taking it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll continue your prednisone. We’ll manage all your regular meds while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just updating you—we’re about to start the procedure now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back in your room. The surgery went well. We successfully revised the tibial component of your right knee. No complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Is the new part secure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s stable. We also did an X-ray after surgery—everything looks good, no issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. My knee feels heavy, but not too painful right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on a PCA pump for pain—press the button when you need relief. We’ll switch to oral meds tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The post-op X-ray confirms the implant is in the right position with normal surgical changes in the soft tissues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. Any sign of infection in the wound?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at all. The dressing is clean. We also took a swab to check for staph—results will be back tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs came back—your hemoglobin is a bit low at 8.5, but we’re watching it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the surgery? I’ve had anemia before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely, yes. But it’s stable. We’ll keep an eye on it and make sure you’re eating well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my blood sugar was high yesterday—should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was 126—slightly elevated, but not unusual after surgery and on steroids. We’ll monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—the staph swab came back negative. No staph aureus detected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a huge relief. I was really worried about infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We are too, given your history. But everything looks clean so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started you on Lovenox today to prevent blood clots. You’re also wearing compression stockings.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had DVT before, so I know how important that is.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re taking every precaution. Physical therapy will also start tomorrow to help you move safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your labs improved—hemoglobin is now 9.4, and your electrolytes are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I’m feeling stronger today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. PT saw you yesterday and says you’re doing well with transfers and walking short distances with a walker.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s tough, but I’m trying. How much weight can I put on the leg?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can bear weight as tolerated—whatever feels comfortable. No restrictions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the dressing—can I get it wet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. Keep the Silverlon dressing dry. You can shower five days after surgery, so that’s tomorrow, but don’t soak the knee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the staples—when do they come out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In about three weeks at your follow-up. The wound looks great—scant drainage, no redness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been icing it like they said. Helps with the swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Keep doing that—20 minutes at a time, especially after PT.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, we’re clearing you for discharge today. You’re doing really well—afebrile, eating, moving, and pain is controlled with oral meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Where am I going? Home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go to a rehab facility for a short stay—about a month. They’ll help with therapy and monitoring your recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What meds am I taking now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue your regular meds: albuterol, metoprolol, prednisone, and cephalexin. For pain, oxycodone every 3 hours as needed, plus acetaminophen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Lovenox?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, injectable Lovenox daily for four weeks to prevent clots. And keep wearing the compression stockings for six weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When do I see the surgeon again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In three weeks. Call the office to confirm. They’ll check the wound and remove the staples.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if something goes wrong before then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Go to the ER or call us if you have fever over 101.5, increased redness, swelling, drainage, or pain that doesn’t improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no driving, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. Not until the surgeon clears you. The oxycodone also means no driving or heavy machinery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be careful. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You’ve done really well. Rehab will help you regain strength. We’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m hopeful this will finally help me walk without pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal. With your commitment and rehab, I’m optimistic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep icing and doing my exercises.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And drink plenty of fluids—helps with constipation from the pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have stool softeners, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, docusate and senna. Use them as needed. Bisacodyl if you’re still constipated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll stay on top of that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. The transport team will take you to rehab in a couple of hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Patel. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you at your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll call to confirm the appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Stay safe and keep up the good work.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of chronic right knee pain due to mechanical loosening of a prior knee replacement underwent revision surgery to replace the tibial component. The procedure was performed without complications, and she tolerated it well. Postoperatively, she was managed with pain control, DVT prophylaxis with Lovenox, and physical therapy. Wound checks showed no signs of infection, and a staph swab was negative. Her hemoglobin improved from 8.5 to 9.4 g/dL during the stay. She was discharged to a rehab facility in stable condition with instructions for wound care, activity as tolerated, and follow-up in three weeks for staple removal. Discharge medications included oxycodone, acetaminophen, cephalexin, prednisone, metoprolol, albuterol, and enoxaparin for four weeks.
